    MA3700 · AIRCRAFT STRUCTURES 1

    Deflection and Buckling

    #Deflection of Beams

    #Boundary Conditions

    Boundary conditions for a fixed support:

    • Zero deflection, u=0 and v=0
    • Zero slope, ∂z∂v​=θ=0

    Boundary conditions for a simple support:

    • Zero deflection, u=0 and v=0

    Boundary conditions for a roller support:

    • Zero deflection, v=0

    Note that both fixed and simple supports restrict movement in horizontal and vertical directions, thus u=0 and v=0 respectively. For a roller support, movement is only restricted in one direction.

    #Symmetrical Section

    Taking summation of forces,

    Sy​+p dz=Sy​+∂z∂Sy​​dz

    p=∂z∂Sy​​

    where p is the load applied on the element

    Taking moments about A,

    M+Sy​ dz=p dz(21​dz)+(M+∂z∂M​dz)

    Sy​ dz=21​p d2z+∂z∂M​dz

    Sy​=∂z∂M​

    The term d2z is very small and can be neglected.

    Comparing the equilibrium equations,

    💡
    p=∂z∂Sy​​=∂z2∂2M​

    When a beam is subjected to bending,
    the strain experienced by the beam is,

    ε=dzdΔ​=Eσ​=EIMc​

    From geometry of the beam,

    Arc Length=rθ

    dΔ=c dθ

    Comparing the above equations,

    dzc dθ​=EIMc​

    dzdθ​=EIM​

    Assuming small angle approximation,

    tanθ≈θ=dzdv​

    dzd​(dzdv​)=EIM​

    dz2d2v​=EIM​

    💡
    EI dz2d2v​=M

    where v is the deflection (displacement in the y-direction)

    Differentiating the deflection equation further,

    EI ∂z4∂4v​=∂z2∂2​M

    💡
    EI ∂z4∂4v​=∂z∂Sy​​=p

    where I is the moment of inertia about the bending axis

    Integrating once, we obtain the equation for shear force,

    EI⋅Sy​=EI ∂z3∂3v​=∫p dz+C1​

    Integrating twice, we obtain the equation for moment,

    EI⋅M=EI ∂z2∂2v​=∬p dz+C1​z+C2​

    Integrating thrice, we obtain the equation for slope,

    EI⋅θ=EI ∂z∂v​=∭p dz+21​C1​z2+C2​z+C3​

    Integrating four times, we obtain the equation for deflection v,

    EI⋅v=∬∬p dz+61​C1​z3+21​C2​z2+C3​z+C4​

    #Example

    Since the section is symmetrical, Ixy​=0.

    Ixx​=∑Br​yr​2

    Ixx​=4(300×10−6)(0.2)2

    Ixx​=48×10−6 m4

    Deflection due to bending

    Cutting the beam at a distance z from the free end,

    M=4800z

    Equation for slope of the beam is,

    EIxx​ ∂z2∂2v​=M=4800z

    EIxx​ ∂z∂v​=∫4800z dz

    EIxx​ ∂z∂v​=2400z2+C1​

    Equation for deflection of the beam is,

    EIxx​ vb​=∫2400z2+C1​ dz

    EIxx​ vb​=800z3+C1​z+C2​

    Boundary conditions:

    • At z=2 m, deflection v=0
    • At z=2 m, slope ∂z∂v​=0

    Substituting the above conditions into the equations,

    C1​=−9600

    C2​=12800

    Deflection at free end of cantilever,

    EIxx​ vb​=800(0)3−9600(0)+12800

    vb​=EIxx​12800​

    vb​=3.81 mm

    Deflection due to shear

    tanγ≈γ=Lvs​​

    Gτ​=Lvs​​

    GAP​=Lvs​​

    vs​=GAPL​

    Recall that τ=Gγ.

    Considering shear flow in the web only,

    vs​=GAPL​

    vs​=(30×109)(0.4×0.001)4800(2)​

    vs​=0.8 mm

    Total deflection is then,

    v=vb​+vs​

    v=3.81+0.8

    v=4.61 mm

    #Arbitrary Section

    Consider a section of an unsymmetrical beam. Deflection can occur along the
    horizontal and vertical directions. Let the absolute deflection, normal to the
    neutral axis of the section, be Δ.

    From symmetrical bending theory,

    M=EIκ=EI⋅R1​

    Comparing with the deflection equation,

    M=EI⋅R1​=EI dz2d2v​

    Substituting deflection v with absolute deflection Δ,

    R1​=dz2d2Δ​

    Position of the displaced point C′ is given by,

    v=−Δcosα ⟶ Δ=−cosαv​

    u=−Δsinα ⟶ Δ=−sinαu​

    Substituting Δ into the radius of curvature,

    R1​=dz2d2​⋅−cosαv​ ⟶ dz2d2v​=−Rcosα​

    R1​=dz2d2​⋅−sinαu​ ⟶ dz2d2u​=−Rsinα​

    At some point dA of the section, strain is given by,

    εz​=κy=Ry​=Rζ​

    where ζ is the perpendicular distance to the neutral axis

    Perpendicular distance of dA to the neutral axis is,

    ζ=xsinα+ycosα

    Bending stress at dA is then,

    σz​=Eεz​=E⋅Rζ​

    σz​=RE​(xsinα+ycosα)

    Moments resulting in the bending stress are,

    Mx​=∫σz​y dA=∫RE​(xysinα+y2cosα) dA

    My​=∫σz​x dA=∫RE​(x2sinα+xycosα) dA

    Recall that Ixx​=∫y2 dA, Iyy​=∫x2 dA, and Ixy​=∫xy dA.

    Mx​=RE​(Ixy​sinα+Ixx​cosα)

    My​=RE​(Iyy​sinα+Ixy​cosα)

    Solving the equations simultaneously,

    💡
    dz2d2u​=−Rsinα​=−E(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2)My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​
    💡
    dz2d2v​=−Rcosα​=−E(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2)Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​​

    Rearranging the equations,

    💡
    Mx​=−EIxx​ dz2d2v​−EIxy​ dz2d2u​
    💡
    My​=−EIyy​ dz2d2u​−EIxy​ dz2d2v​

    If the section has an axis of symmetry,

    💡
    Mx​=−EIxx​ dz2d2v​
    💡
    My​=−EIyy​ dz2d2u​

    #Example

    Sectional Properties

    Ixx​=12t(2a)3​+2[12at3​+at(a)2]+2[12t(a/2)3​+2at​(43​)2]=413​a3t

    Iyy​=122at3​+2[12ta3​+at(2a​)2]+2[12(a/2)t3​+2at​(a)2]=35​a3t

    Ixy​=∑Axy=−47​a3t

    Iˉxx​=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Ixx​​=113a3t156​

    Iˉyy​=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Iyy​​=113a3t80​

    Iˉxy​=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Ixy​​=−113a3t84​

    Deflection due to Bending

    Taking moments about D,

    P(3L)=Rb​(2L)

    Rb​=23​P

    Rd​=−21​P

    Cutting the beam at a distance z from support D,

    Mx​=Rd​z=−21​Pz

    Note that there is only bending about the x-axis.
    There is no bending moment about the     y-axis.

    Horizontal deflection of beam

    Equation for the horizontal deflection of the beam is,

    dz2d2u​=−E(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2)My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​

    dz2d2u​=−E(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2)−Mx​Ixy​​

    dz2d2u​=EMx​​Iˉxy​

    Bending moment of the beam is,

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 dz2d2u​=Mx​

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 dz2d2u​=−21​Pz

    Slope of the beam is,

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 dzdu​=∫−21​Pz dz

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 dzdu​=−41​Pz2+C1​

    Deflection of the beam is,

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 u=∫−41​Pz2+C1​ dz

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 u=−121​Pz3+C1​z+C2​

    Substituting u=0 at z=0, we get C2​=0.

    Substituting u=0 at z=2L, we get C1​=3PL2​.

    Recall that for simple supports, deflection is zero at the supports.

    Horizontal deflection at the midpoint of B and D,

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 u=−121​Pz3+3PL2​z

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 u=−121​PL3+31​PL3

    E(Iˉxy​)−1 u=41​PL3

    u=4EPL3​Iˉxy​

    u=4EPL3​(−113a3t84​)

    u=−113a3t21PL3​

    Vertical deflection of beam

    Equation for the vertical deflection of the beam is,

    dz2d2v​=−E(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2)Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​​

    dz2d2v​=−E(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2)Mx​Iyy​​

    dz2d2v​=−EMx​​Iˉyy​

    Bending moment is,

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 dz2d2v​=Mx​

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 dz2d2v​=−21​Pz

    Slope of the beam is,

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 dzdv​=∫−21​Pz dz

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 dzdv​=−41​Pz2+C1​

    Deflection of the beam is,

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 v=∫−41​Pz2+C1​ dz

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 v=−121​Pz3+C1​z+C2​

    Substituting v=0 at z=0, we get C2​=0.

    Substituting v=0 at z=2L, we get C1​=3PL2​.

    Recall that for simple supports, deflection is zero at the supports.

    Vertical deflection at the midpoint of B and D,

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 v=−121​Pz3+3PL2​z

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 v=−121​PL3+31​PL3

    −E(Iˉyy​)−1 v=41​PL3

    v=−4EPL3​Iˉyy​

    v=−4EPL3​(113a3t80​)

    v=−113a3t20PL3​

    #Unit Load Method

    Consider a beam subjected to a steadily increasing load P. As the beam extends, the load does work, and from the law of conservation of energy, this work is stored in the beam as strain energy.

    Work done during an increase in deflection δΔ
    can be approximated as (assuming P is constant),

    δW=P(δΔ)

    Complementary work done during an increase
    in load δP can be approximated as (assuming deflection Δ is constant),

    δWvirtual​=Δ(δP)

    Complementary strain energy during an increase
    in stress δσ can be approximated as (assuming strain ε is constant),

    δUvirtal​=∫ε(δσ) dV

    Equating virtual work to strain energy,

    Δ(δP)=∫ε(δσ) dV

    Since δP is a virtual load, let δP=1. Equations
    for the real deflection due to bending and shear
    can then be obtained.

    Deflection due to bending is given by,

    💡
    Δ=∫ε(δσ) dV

    Deflection due to shear is given by,

    💡
    Δ=∫γ(δτ) dV

    Recall that in the elastic region, σ=Eε and τ=Gγ.

    Δ=∫Eσ​(δσ) dV=∬Eσ​(δσ) dAdz

    Δ=∫Gτ​(δτ) dV=∬Gτ​(δτ) dAdz

    #Unit Load Equations for the Different Loads

    For an axial load, actual stress is σ=AP​, and virtual stress is δσ=Ap​.

    💡
    ΔP​=∫0L​EAPp​ dz

    where P is the actual load, and p is the virtual load

    For a bending load, actual stress is σ=IMy​, and virtual stress is δσ=Imy​.

    💡
    ΔM​=∫0L​⟨EIMm​⟩ dz

    where M is the actual moment, and m is the virtual moment

    For shear forces, actual stress is τ=tQs​​, and virtual stress is τ=tqs​​.

    💡
    ΔQ​=∫0L​(∫GtQs​qs​​ ds)dz

    where Qs​ is the actual shear flow, and qs​ is the virtual shear flow

    For torque, actual stress is τ=JTa​r​, and virtual stress is JTv​r​.

    💡
    ΔT​=∫0L​GJTa​Tv​​ dz

    where Ta​ is the actual torque, and Tv​ is the virtual torque

    #Unit Load Equation for Bending Deflection

    Recall from unsymmetrical bending theory,

    σz​=(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​)x+(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​​)y

    σz​=(My​Iˉxx​−Mx​Iˉxy​)x+(Mx​Iˉyy​−My​Iˉxy​)y

    Virtual stress is then,

    δσz​=(my​Iˉxx​−mx​Iˉxy​)x+(mx​Iˉyy​−my​Iˉxy​)y

    Substituting into the unit load equation for bending,

    ΔM​=∬Eσ​(δσ) dAdz

    ΔM​=E1​∬σ(δσ) dAdz

    ΔM​=E1​∬[(Mx​Iˉyy​−My​Iˉxy​)(mx​Iˉyy​−my​Iˉxy​)y2                        +(My​Iˉxx​−Mx​Iˉxy​)(my​Iˉxx​−mx​Iˉxy​)x2                        +(Mx​Iˉyy​−My​Iˉxy​)(mx​Iˉyy​−my​Iˉxy​)xy                        +(My​Iˉxx​−Mx​Iˉxy​)(my​Iˉxx​−mx​Iˉxy​)xy] dAdz

    ΔM​=E1​∬[(Mx​Iˉyy​−My​Iˉxy​)(mx​Iˉyy​−my​Iˉxy​)Iyy​                        +(My​Iˉxx​−Mx​Iˉxy​)(my​Iˉxx​−mx​Iˉxy​)Ixx​                        +(Mx​Iˉyy​−My​Iˉxy​)(mx​Iˉyy​−my​Iˉxy​)Ixy​                        +(My​Iˉxx​−Mx​Iˉxy​)(my​Iˉxx​−mx​Iˉxy​)Ixy​] dz

    For a section with an axis of symmetry,

    💡
    ΔM​=E1​∫Ixx​Mx​mx​​+Iyy​My​my​​ dz

    #Combined Deflection

    Recall from practical aircraft stress analysis,

    Qs​−Q0​=−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sy​Iyy​−Sx​Ixy​​) ∑Br​yr​−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sx​Ixx​−Sy​Ixy​​) ∑Br​xr​

    Qs​−Q0​=−(Sy​Iˉyy​−Sx​Iˉxy​) ∑Br​yr​−(Sx​Iˉxx​−Sy​Iˉxy​) ∑Br​xr​

    Virtual shear flow is then,

    qs​−q0​=−(Vy​Iˉyy​−Vx​Iˉxy​) ∑Br​yr​−(Vx​Iˉxx​−Vy​Iˉxy​) ∑Br​xr​

    Note that for an open section beam, Q0​=q0​=0.

    The combined deflection due to bending and shear is then,

    💡
    Δcomb​=∫0L​⟨EIMm​⟩ dz+∫0L​(∫GtQs​qs​​ ds)dz

    #Example

    General equation for shear flow for an idealized section,

    qs​−q0​=−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sy​Iyy​−Sx​Ixy​​) ∑Br​yr​−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sx​Ixx​−Sy​Ixy​​) ∑Br​xr​

    Since the cantilever has an open section, shear flow q0​=0,
    and the section has an axis of symmetry,     Ixy​=0. There is
    only shear force in the vertical direction, thus     Sx​=0.

    Ixx​=∑Br​yr​2

    Ixx​=4[300(200)2]

    Ixx​=48×106 mm4

    Let Qs​ be the actual shear flow.

    Qs​=−Ixx​Sy​​∑Br​yr​

    Qs​=−48×1064800​∑Br​yr​

    Let qs​ be the virtual shear flow.

    qs​=−Ixx​1​∑Br​yr​

    qs​=−48×1061​∑Br​yr​

    qs​=4800Q​

    Actual shear flow

    Actual shear flow in wall 1-2 is,

    Q12​=−48×1064800​(B1​y1​)

    Q12​=−48×1064800​(300)(200)

    Q12​=−6 N/mm

    Actual shear flow in wall 2-3 is,

    Q23​=Q12​−48×1064800​(B2​y2​)

    Q23​=−6−48×1064800​(300)(200)

    Q23​=−12 N/mm

    Actual shear flow in wall 3-4 is,

    Q34​=Q23​−48×1064800​(B3​y3​)

    Q34​=−12−48×1064800​(300)(−200)

    Q34​=−6 N/mm

    Total deflection

    Δcomb​=Δbending​+Δshear​

    Δcomb​=∫0L​EIMm​ dz+∫0L​(∫GtQs​qs​​ ds)dz

    Combined deflection due to bending and shear.

    Bending Moment

    Actual system: M=4800z

    Unit load: m=1z

    ΔM​=∫0L​EIMm​ dz

    ΔM​=∫02000​(70×103)(48×106)4800z2​ dz

    ΔM​=(70×103)(48×106)4800​[31​z3]02000​

    ΔM​=3.81 mm

    Shear

    Actual system: Qs​=−48×1064800​∑Br​yr​

    Unit load: qs​=4800Q​

    ΔQ​=∫0L​(∫GtQs​qs​​ ds)dz

    ΔQ​=(30×103)(1)1​∫02000​(∫4800Qs​2​ ds)dz

    ΔQ​=4800(30×103)1​∫02000​ Q12​2L12​+Q23​2L23​+Q34​2L34​ dz

    ΔQ​=4800(30×103)1​∫02000​ 2(−6)2(200)+(−12)2(400) dz

    ΔQ​=4800(30×103)72000(2000)​

    ΔQ​=1 mm

    Combined Deflection

    Total deflection is then,

    Δcomb​=3.81+1=4.81 mm

    #Buckling of Columns

    Compressive stresses within a long, thin structure can cause structural instability or buckling. Local buckling may cause permanent deformation but global buckling can be catastrophic.

    #Euler Buckling Load

    Consider a perfect column (ideally straight), simply supported at both ends, experiences buckling. The deflection of the beam, where it has buckled, can be determined using the deflection equation.

    EI ∂z2∂2v​=−Pcr​v

    EI ∂z2∂2v​+Pcr​v=0

    ∂z2∂2v​+λ2v=0

    where λ2=EIPcr​​

    The solution to the homogeneous
    ordinary differential equation is,

    v=Acosλz+Bsinλz

    where A and B are deflection coefficients

    Applying the boundary conditions,

    At z=0, v=0, thus A=0.
    At z=L, v=0, thus BsinλL=0.

    where λL=π,2π, ⋯=mπ, and m indicates the buckling mode

    Substituting λL=mπ into the buckling load,

    (Lmπ​)2=EIPcr​​

    Pcr​=(Lmπ​)2EI

    Minimum critical buckling load is when m=1, which is also known as Euler’s load.

    💡
    PEuler​=L2π2​EI

    By adding additional constraints to the column to restrict deflection at a certain location, the critical buckling load increases.

    💡
    Pcr​=L2m2π2​EI=m2⋅PEuler​

    The addition of ribs along the span of the wing introduces additional constraints to the skin, increasing the skin’s critical buckling load.

    For columns with different end conditions, the above equation is modified.

    💡
    Pcr​=KL2m2π2​EI=Km2⋅PEuler​

    • Fixed at both ends (C-C), K=4
    • Simply supported at both ends (S-S), K=1
    • Fixed at one end and free at the other (C-F), K=0.25
    • Simply supported at one end and fixed at the other (C-S), K=2.05

    #Effect of Initial Imperfections

    In practice, ideally straight columns do not exist. Imperfections exist in the shape of
    the column and loading eccentricities. Thus, the load at which the column buckles
    can be less than its critical buckling load.

    Consider a column, simply supported at both ends,
    is initially bent. Initial imperfection of the column is assumed to be,

    💡
    v0​=a0​sinLπz​

    From the deflection equation,

    EI ∂z2∂2v​=−P(v+v0​)

    EI ∂z2∂2v​+Pv=−Pv0​

    ∂z2∂2v​+λ2v=−λ2v0​

    where λ2=EIP​

    The solution to the homogeneous
    ordinary differential equation is,

    v=Acosλz+Bsinλz+CsinLπz​

    where A, B, and C are deflection coefficients

    Derivatives of the solution are then,

    ∂z∂v​=−Aλsinλz+Bλcosλz+C(Lπ​)cosLπz​

    ∂z2∂2v​=−Aλ2cosλz−Bλ2sinλz−C(Lπ​)2sinLπz​

    Substituting the above into the differential equation,

    ∂z2∂2v​+λ2v=−λ2v0​

    −C(Lπ​)2sinLπz​+Cλ2sinLπz​=−λ2a0​sinLπz​

    C[(Lπ​)2−λ2]=λ2a0​

    C=(π/λL)2−1a0​​

    Rearranging Euler’s equation for a perfect column hinged at both ends,

    L2π2​=EIPEuler​​

    The term in the denominator of coefficient C differs by λ21​.

    λ21​⋅L2π2​=λ21​⋅EIPEuler​​

    λ2L2π2​=P/EI1​⋅EIPEuler​​

    (λLπ​)2=PPEuler​​

    💡
    α1​=PPEuler​​

    Ratio of Euler buckling load (perfect column) with the
    actual buckling load of a column with imperfections.

    Applying the boundary conditions,

    At z=0, v=0, thus A=0.
    At z=L, v=0, thus BsinλL=0.

    Note that since sinλL=0 is the solution for a Euler column, then B=0, as we
    are only interested in obtaining a different solution for a column with imperfections.

    The solution to the homogeneous ordinary differential equation is,

    v=CsinLπz​

    v=(π/λL)2−1a0​​sinLπz​

    v=1/α−1a0​​sinLπz​

    💡
    v=1−αα​a0​sinLπz​

    Total deflection, which includes the initial imperfection v0​, is then,

    vtot​=v0​+v

    vtot​=a0​sinLπz​+1−αα​a0​sinLπz​

    💡
    vtot​=1−α1​a0​sinLπz​

    Let the deflection at the midpoint of the column, hinged at both ends, be δ=vtot​.

    Substituting z=2L​ into δ,

    δ=1−α1​a0​sinLπ(L/2)​

    δ=1−αa0​​

    α=1−δa0​​

    PEuler​P​=1−δa0​​

    It can be seen that if the initial imperfection is very small, that is a0​→0, the actual buckling load P of the column can be approximated to be equal to Euler buckling
    load PEuler​. Thus, Euler’s equation can be used instead if imperfections are minor.

    #Analysis of Beam Columns

    Beam columns are structural members that support both axial and transverse loads.
    Consider a beam column with a concentrated transverse load W and axial load P.

    From the deflection equation,

    EI ∂z2∂2v​=−Pv−21​Wz

    EI ∂z2∂2v​+Pv=−21​Wz

    ∂z2∂2v​+λ2v=−2EIW​z

    where λ2=EIP​

    The solution to the homogeneous
    ordinary differential equation is,

    v=Acosλz+Bsinλz+Cz

    where A, B, and C are deflection coefficients

    Derivatives of the solution are then,

    ∂z∂v​=−Aλsinλz+Bλcosλz+C

    ∂z2∂2v​=−Aλ2cosλz−Bλ2sinλz

    Substituting the above into the differential equation,

    ∂z2∂2v​+λ2v=−2EIW​z

    λ2Cz=−2EIW​z

    C=−2EIλ2W​

    C=−2PW​

    Boundary conditions of beam column:

    • At z=0, deflection v=0, thus A=0
    • At z=2L​, slope ∂z∂v​=0 at the point of maximum deflection

    Substituting the boundary conditions,

    ∂z∂v​=−Aλsinλz+Bλcosλz+C

    0=Bλcos2λL​−2PW​

    B=2Pλcos(λL/2)W​

    Deflection at a given point is then,

    v=Acosλz+Bsinλz+Cz

    v=2Pλcos(λL/2)W​sinλz−2PW​z

    💡
    v=2PλW​[cos(λL/2)sinλz​−λz]

    Let the deflection at the midpoint, z=2L​, of the beam be δ=v.

    δ=2PλW​[cos(λL/2)sin(λL/2)​−2λL​]

    δ=2PλW​(tanβ−β)

    where β=2λL​

    By expressing tanβ as its Maclaurin series and β in terms of P and PEuler​,

    δ=48EIWL3​⋅1−P/PEuler​1​

    💡
    δ=kW​⋅1−α1​

    where W is the concentrated transverse load and stiffness k=L348EI​

    The relationship between W and δ is linear, even when the axial load P=0.
    The relationship between α and δ is non-linear, similar to that of an imperfect column.

    #Energy Approach to Buckling

    A conservative system is in equilibrium when the energy stored is equal to the work done by the external loads. Consider a virtual increment of displacement as a result of a load.
    The external work done is dWe​, and the strain energy stored during deformation is dU.

    dU=dWe​

    dU−dWe​=0

    d(U−We​)=0

    Total potential energy Π of the system is a constant.

    💡
    Π=U−We​

    Elastic strain energy of an element dz in a column is,

    dU=21​σz​εz​ dV

    U=21​∭σz​εz​ dxdydz

    U=21​∬Eσz​2​ dAdz

    Substituting σ=IMy​ and EI ∂z2∂2v​=M into the above equation,

    U=21​∬E1​(IMy​)2 dAdz

    U=2E1​∬(EI ∂z2∂2v​)2I2y2​ dAdz

    U=2E1​∫(EI ∂z2∂2v​)2I1​ dz

    U=21​∫EI(∂z2∂2v​)2 dz

    Consider an element on the y-z plane being deformed by a force Pcr​. Work done by the force is,

    dWe​=Pcr​ dw

    dWe​=Pcr​[dz−(dz)2−(∂z∂v​dz)2​ ]

    dWe​=Pcr​⋅21​(∂z∂v​)2dz

    We​=21​∫Pcr​(∂z∂v​)2 dz

    Total potential energy in the buckled system is then,

    💡
    Π=21​∫EI(∂z2∂2v​)2 dz−21​∫Pcr​(∂z∂v​)2 dz

    Solutions to the total potential energy equation:

    • S-S boundary conditions, v=sinLmπz​ where m=1,2,3,...
    • C-C boundary conditions, v=sinLπz​sinLmπz​ where m=1,2,3,...
    • C-S boundary conditions, v=sin2Lπz​sin2Lmπz​ where m=2,4,6,...

    The above solutions are also known as the admissible deflection functions.

    #Example

    Consider a simply supported beam column subjected to compression.

    Assume the admissible function of the beam is v=AsinLπz​.

    Derivatives of the admissible function are,

    ∂z∂v​=A(Lπ​)cosLπz​

    ∂z2∂2v​=−A(Lπ​)2sinLπz​

    Apply the boundary conditions,

    At z=0, v=Asin0=0.
    At z=L, v=Asinπ=0.

    Thus, the admissible function satisfies the boundary conditions.

    Elastic strain energy of the beam column is,

    U=21​∫0L​EI[−A(Lπ​)2sinLπz​]2 dz

    U=2EI​A2(Lπ​)4∫0L​sin2Lπz​ dz

    U=2EI​A2(Lπ​)4(2L​)

    Work done by the external force Pcr​ is,

    We​=21​∫0L​Pcr​[A(Lπ​)cosLπz​]2 dz

    We​=2Pcr​​A2(Lπ​)2∫0L​cos2Lπz​ dz

    We​=2Pcr​​A2(Lπ​)2(2L​)

    Total potential energy of the beam is then,

    Π=2EI​A2(Lπ​)4(2L​)−2Pcr​​A2(Lπ​)2(2L​)

    Differentiating with respect to A,

    ∂A∂Π​=EI⋅A(Lπ​)4(2L​)−Pcr​⋅A(Lπ​)2(2L​)

    0=EI⋅A(Lπ​)4(2L​)−Pcr​⋅A(Lπ​)2(2L​)

    Note that since Π is a constant, its derivative is zero.

    Rearranging the above equation,

    EI⋅A(Lπ​)4(2L​)=Pcr​⋅A(Lπ​)2(2L​)

    EI(Lπ​)2=Pcr​

    Pcr​=L2π2​EI

    Solving for Pcr​ gives the Euler buckling load (exact solution). The result of the energy approach is exact as the chosen function satisfies the boundary conditions. Thus, the chosen function gives the exact deflected shape of the beam column.
